abstract: Learning from continuous material involves dynamic coordination of visual sampling, autonomic arousal, and neural activity, yet how these signals jointly organize during successful learning remains unclear. Here, we analysed synchronized eye-tracking, pupillometry, and EEG recordings from 86 participants from the Brain, Body, and Behavior Dataset. Using hidden Markov modelling, we identified recurrent multimodal states after accounting for stable recording-level differences and stimulus-shared responses. Three reproducible states with distinct psychophysiological profiles emerged. Poorer subsequent quiz performance was associated with greater relative expression of a state characterized by longer fixations, reduced fixation and saccade rates, lower gaze entropy, elevated pupil level and variability, and distinct EEG spectral entropy and frontoparietal theta coherence. In contrast, better performance was associated with greater expression of a state characterized primarily by more frequent and larger phasic pupil dilations. Quiz performance was also positively associated with transitions from this phasic-pupil state to the dominant background state, whereas relative expression of the dominant state itself showed no robust association with performance. The transition association did not survive correction in common-record window-length sensitivity analyses. These findings indicate that learning during naturalistic viewing is associated with the dynamic coordination of multiple ocular, pupillary, and neural signals, with relative state balance and directed transition probabilities each associated with subsequent quiz performance.
